chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from Suwayd ibn Sa'id al-Qalla' from Ayub from Abi Basir from Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Indeed, when the people of the Torah and the people of the Gospel come to him to refer their disputes to him, it is up to him; if he wishes, he judges between them, and if he wishes, he leaves them.
ai.seo_question: What is the judge's discretion when non-Muslims seek legal judgment?
ai.summary: In the context of Shia jurisprudence, this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the discretionary power (*ikhtiyar*) of the Imam or judge when non-Muslims voluntarily seek his arbitration, distinguishing it from obligatory application of Sharia. It underscores that the judge may choose to rule based on his own judgment or decline jurisdiction, reflecting the flexibility in managing pluralistic legal systems under Islamic governance. This ruling is often cited to support the validity of *dhimmi* courts or the judge's choice in applying Islamic law versus the communities' own laws in civil matters.
